entry.title: My First Published Research Paper!
entry.content:
Motivation

The reason behind me writing this blog is mainly to refresh my thoughts and my experiences of being on a published paper. I want to be able to explain what this paper was about as well as my contribution to this paper, and what my thoughts were during the process of being apart of this project.

Introduction

I first got onto this project from an invitation from a friend who needed help with this research project, Rohan Yelandur. So, I would like to first express my gratitude to him for giving me the opportunity to join this project and be apart of a published paper! At first when I joined the project, initially all I thought I would be doing was doing data collection for a Franka Panda Robot Arm, using a space mouse. Rohan got me caught up with all of the onboarding of the project, which included learning how to use the spacemouse, how to boot up the robot, and how to run the data collection pipeline scripts. I didn’t meet frequently with the main mastermind behind the project, Shivin, until summer hit.

What the paper was about

Now, time to get into the techincal details of this paper. I will explain this as concisely as I can using the Fei-Fei Li Black Box.

What is the problem we are trying to solve?

Say you want to collect robot data in a particular environment so the robot can be deployed there, but collecting data in that environment is impractical due to a couple of potential reasons such as: privacy (collecting data in the consumer’s home), safety, cost, and plain access. However, we have alternative environments where data collection is easier, such as lab spaces and mock setups such as apartments or kitchens. These are useful, but they aren’t as useful as the target environment.

So the real problem we are trying to solve is “what data should we collect in the accessible environments so that it transfers best to the deployment task?”

Why is SOTA not enough?

In the modern state-of-the-art (SOTA), robot data collection is mostly unguided. Teleoperators collect data based on their intution, and much of that data ends up being wasted as it contributes little to the final policy. Also, the enviroment you collect data in matters as well.

The default answer in robot learning has been to collect broadly and rely on scale. However, recent work has shown us that carefully curated datasets can beat much larger, unfiltered ones when targeting a specific downstream domain, which tells us that not all demonstrations are equally useful. However, we can only know which subsets of data are good only after we’ve collected all of the data, so the time and labor of collecting that data has already been paid.

We want to move data collection upstream: instead of filtering data after collection, we guid humans toward collecting the most useful demonstrations at the start.

What is our clever idea?

We propose Guided Data Collection (GDC), which asks which data to collect in the data collection environments to maximize performance on the deployment task.

We are given: $\mathcal{D}$: the current dataset,

$\mathcal{D}’$: the new data to collect in data collection environments, under a fixed budget $k=|\mathcal{D}’|$,

$\mathcal{A}$: the learning algorithm, which maps a dataset to a policy $\pi = \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D})$,

$\mathcal{M}$: the performance metric, which measures a deployment performance of a policy (e.g., success rate).

The goal is to find the new data that improves the policy once it is added to the training set: \(argmax_{\mathcal{D}'} \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D} \cup \mathcal{D}')) \ s.t \ |\mathcal{D}'| = k\)

How will we evaluate it?

GUILD splits this problem into $2$ pieces and interleaves them in a close loop: task-space exploration using a VLM (Chat-GPT 5.2), which decides where it could be worth collecting data, and data evaluation using predictive data attribution[^1], which decides how much data each of those tasks deserves.

Commonsense-grounded task proposals

GUILD gives the VLM the target-domain context (a demonstration video, a language description of the target task and a specification of available environments and objects) and asks it to propose a set of feasbile collection tasks. Each proposal specifies which environment to collect in, and how to set up the scene and what manipulation task to demonstrate.

Something to note, the VLM is not asked how much data to collect per task. It only defines the support of the collection distribution, i.e. the promising regions of the task space.

Data evaluation via predictive attribution

After a few demonstrations are collected for each proposed task, GUILD estimates how useful each trajectory is for the deployment without training and rolling out a new policy for every candidate dataset. We use MAGIC, a metagradient-based data attribution method.

Iterate on two timescales

GUILD collects data in small batches and recomputes utilities after every batch:

  • Inner loop (redefine the distribution): Compute the utility for every task in the current support, ask the teleoperator to collect a small batch, add it to the dataset, repeat
  • Outer loop (expand support): every $K$ inner steps, query the VLM again, this time also giving it the ranked list of previously evaluated tasks. This feedback steers new proposals toward regions related to high-utility tasks, while still allowing genuinely new ideas.

Closing Thoughts

Ok, now that I’ve explained the project, now I can get what I learned implicitly from research. The first thing I want to start off with is that I respect PhD students and research scientists even more now after doing a project like this, because this was very tough mentally. Specifically, the hard part about this project was showing up to the lab which had limited light coming through and just sitting at the desk, collecting data and doing evaluations of policies for $10$+ hours a day.

Maybe this was just a very labor-intensive project, but still it was hard mentally to take a break from time to time because I felt the pressure to continue to work as fast as possible, especially because my work was the main part of the project, and without it the paper wouldn’t have been published in time. (It didn’t help that Shivin and Rohan left early for their internships, leaving me to take the real-world experiments to the finish line)

This made me realize if I really wanted to pursue a PhD or not, something I’m still thinking about as I write this. However, I’m glad I was able to push through and get the project done, as our paper got published and accepted to the Conference of Robot Learning (CoRL ‘26)! I was able to go to this conference and experience my very first conference, which is something that was really cool to experience.

I’m definitely going to try another project to really see if the path of research is for me. I’ll also try to get an internship during this summer to see if I like that, and choose which path I like better.

Also I realize Shivin made a whole website about GUILD, which explains what GUILD does better than I have. I just made this post to explain GUILD in my own words so that I can remember it better.

That’s all I have to write about for right now, I’ll see you in the next blog post!

entry.title: Persistence is Key
entry.content:
I’m mainly writing this to express my feelings on rejection and failure, hopefully so that when I look back on this in the future I can look back at this post and smile and appreciate how far I’ve come. But as of right now, I am currently a sophmore CS major, with nothing lined up for the summer and a complicated family situation.

Being lost and rejected

I’m currently lost as to what I want to do for right now, because SWE feels meaningless to me if I’m not attracted to the goal or purpose of a project of a particular company. I mean sure, interning at Amazon would be nice, but would I feel a sense of passion for programming at Amazon? My current feelings on big tech right now are that I feel like I would just be a cog in the wheel, living monotonously reviewing code and going to weekly meetings. I feel like I would crash out if that were the case. (This is just what I think a day in the life as a swe would be, I have yet to experience that life yet lol). I’m not in the field of CS for the money, I truly do love programming and creating new things, but it’s just hard for me to know what I want to do as I feel like I’ve spent too much time focusing on academics and not enough time researching about career development and what CS is like in the real world. I feel like I spend too much time in the CS building working on academics, but what else is there for me to do really? None of my friends seem to share the same enthusiam I have for CS, and I don’t really have the time to make any side projects as my classes consume the majority of my time.

The things that I would want to go after feel unattainable to me, as you need to be really knowledgeable in that field in order to land a job in said field. For example, lets take robotics. I feel like the bar is so high in order to land a position in the field of robotics, since it is after all an interdisciplinary field, where there are focuses on hardware, software, machine learning and artificial intelligence. And the focuses that I’ve just listed go even deeper, where in machine learning you can do supervised learning, imitation learning, reinforcement learning, on and on. I feel like it’s so hard to pick a niche since this field is so vast.

A part of me feels like I’m too dumb to do the things that I want to go for, but another part of me is confident that I’m smart enough to do the things I want to go for, but I just need to be given a chance, someone to give me a chance to be specific.

I feel like I’m lacking too much as of now, but with the pressure of my family situation I feel like I need to go beyond and not care about my feelings and just get a job to help support my family. I really do feel like I’m rambling now, as I’ve lost the entire point of this article haha.

The persistence part

The main thing I wanted to write down is that even though the feeling of rejection and failure hurts, I still have the passion, strength, and determination to keep pushing forward. I feel like my greatest strength is my stubborness, and every time I face a set back, I use that as fuel to prove my doubts wrong even further. My stubborness also gives me strength to push through even the toughest of times, and I often find myself in positions where I get a helping hand, whether I expect it or not. Maybe it’s God looking out for me, or maybe I’m just in the right place at the right time, or maybe I’m likeable enough where people will go out of their way to help me, who really knows. The main thing is that I will continue to trudge forward, one step at a time, and hopefully my future self will thank me and smile thinking about all of the hard times I endured and be grateful for those times. I hope me in $5$ years knows all of the answers that I currently have about myself. I try not to think too hard about things I can’t control, but I can’t help but think of all the things I could be experiencing/having right now if things were going my way.

I do realize there is more to being successful than your professional career, but I can’t help but look around me and see all of my peers succeeding in that regard, so I do think about what I am lacking that they have, which helps them to succeed more than I do. This post is turning out more depressing than I would’ve liked, I meant for this to be a motivating post that my future self could look back on and smile at!

Alright, enough moping, time to get back to studying for Algorithms and AI. Until next time.
